A staff member offered a gift of more than $10 declines it politely and tells the supervisor. Any gift accepted by mistake is returned or turned over to the Administrator and logged.

Staff do not borrow from, lend to, or sell to an individual, and do not use an individual's money, card, property, vehicle or food for personal use. Personal funds are handled only as FIN-03 describes, with receipts and two-signature controls.

Staff do not contact individuals on personal social media or by personal phone for non-work purposes. They do not post photos, videos or information about individuals. Any photo for agency use requires written consent from the individual or guardian as RTS-05 requires.

Staff do not give rides in personal vehicles, host individuals at their homes, or socialize with individuals outside work except as the Personal Plan or Implementation Strategy authorizes and the Administrator approves in writing.

Staff who feel a personal relationship developing with an individual, or who are asked for personal favors, tell the supervisor right away. The supervisor documents it and decides how to protect both parties, including a reassignment if needed.

Staff never use physical force, threats, humiliation, withholding of food or belongings, seclusion, time-out or aversive procedures. Staff follow the behavior supports in each individual's plan and GPR-03 and GPR-04.
Any staff member who sees or suspects a violation reports it immediately as GPR-05 directs. The reporter is protected from retaliation, and retaliation is itself a violation.

When an allegation is received, the Administrator removes the accused staff member from direct contact with individuals pending investigation, ensures individual safety, and starts the GPR-05 and CI-01 processes. The Administrator notifies the guardian within 24 hours of receiving an allegation of abuse or neglect, as 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320 requires.
The Administrator makes the reports required by CI-02 to law enforcement, the DHS Office of Inspector General and CIRAS, and documents the date, time and person reported to.

After investigation, the Administrator decides on discipline in consultation with Human Resources. Discipline can be coaching, written warning, suspension or termination, depending on severity. Substantiated abuse, neglect or exploitation results in termination unless law requires otherwise.
The Administrator reports substantiated findings to the Health Care Worker Registry or other agencies where Part 50 or registry rules apply, and records the report in the incident file.
Boundary concerns, trends and corrective actions are reviewed in the QA-01 quarterly review and reported to the Governing Body without identifying details that must be kept confidential.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, removes accused staff from contact with individuals, makes required reports, and decides discipline.
Model boundaries, respond to staff concerns, document boundary issues and report suspected violations immediately.
Keep to the boundaries in this policy, report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, and sign the annual acknowledgment.
Files acknowledgments, supports investigations and documents disciplinary action.

documentation: Signed Code of Conduct/boundaries acknowledgments (at hire and annually)
Gift declination and acceptance log
Documentation of boundary concerns and supervisor responses
Allegation, investigation and reporting records (GPR-05, CI-01, CI-02)
Disciplinary records
Training records for TRN-04
QA quarterly review summaries

policies.title: Cumulative Case Records, Personal Plan and Implementation Strategy
policies.applies_to: All individuals served by [AGENCY NAME]; QIDPs, nurses, DSPs, supervisors and the Administrator who create or use case records
policies.purpose: To make sure a complete cumulative case record that includes the Personal Plan and the Implementation Strategy is kept for each individual, is current, and is available at the residence for staff to follow.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(1) — Recordkeeping: Cumulative case records including a Personal Plan and Implementation Strategy shall be maintained for each individual.

[AGENCY NAME] maintains a cumulative case record for each individual from entry through discharge. The record contains the written informed consent to participate, prior service history, the Personal Plan, the Implementation Strategy, assessments, and the other contents described in REC-03. The record follows the Personal Plan requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c)(2), 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.230 and 59 Ill. Adm. Code 120.160.

The Implementation Strategy is on Form IL462-4470 and is developed within 20 calendar days of the provider's dated signature on the Personal Plan. It is based on the Personal Plan and assessments, with the individual and guardian taking part, and with the Independent Service Coordination (ISC) agency as necessary. It addresses the outcomes the agency agreed to support, and it is signed by the individual and guardian. The individual and guardian receive a copy of the strategy and every update. The QIDP reviews the strategy at least monthly and documents the review. See PCS-01 for the planning process and timelines.

The current Personal Plan and Implementation Strategy are kept at the residence where the individual lives, where staff can use them. The records are confidential and protected as REC-01 and RTS-05 describe. This policy also supports the record-content requirements of 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.

definitions.definition: The single organized record for an individual, containing consents, history, assessments, Personal Plan, Implementation Strategy, daily and chronological documentation, and health and incident information.
The person-centered plan developed by the individual, guardian, ISC and team that states the individual's goals, needs, preferences and supports.
The agency's plan on Form IL462-4470 for how it will support the outcomes in the Personal Plan that it agreed to support.
Qualified Intellectual Disability Professional, who leads the Provider Support Team and reviews the Implementation Strategy at least monthly.
Independent Service Coordination agency, which helps the individual develop the Personal Plan and coordinates services.

procedures: At admission, the QIDP opens a cumulative case record with a table of contents. Section headings follow REC-03, including consent, prior service history, Personal Plan, Implementation Strategy, assessments, health, rights, financial and incident sections.

The QIDP confirms the written informed consent to participate is signed by the individual and, where there is one, the guardian, and files it before or at admission. Prior service history is requested from the ISC, former provider and guardian and filed. Missing items are listed with a follow-up date.

When the ISC provides the Personal Plan, the QIDP checks that it is complete and that the agency's dated signature is entered, then files it. The 20-calendar-day period for the Implementation Strategy starts on the date of the provider's signature.

The Provider Support Team, with the individual and guardian (and ISC as necessary), drafts the Implementation Strategy on Form IL462-4470 from the Personal Plan and assessments. It covers the outcomes the agency agreed to support and states the supports, staff, supervision level and any time alone or independent community access, with time periods and locations.

The QIDP obtains the signatures of the individual and guardian on the strategy within 20 calendar days of the provider's signature on the Personal Plan. If signatures are delayed, the QIDP records each attempt and the reason and tells the Administrator.
The QIDP gives the individual and guardian a copy of the Implementation Strategy and each update, in a format the person understands (RTS-04), and records the date and method of delivery.

A current copy of the Personal Plan and Implementation Strategy is placed in the individual's record at the residence on the day they are final. Outdated versions are marked superseded and moved to the archive section of the record.

At least monthly, the QIDP reviews the Implementation Strategy against daily documentation (PCS-03), progress and changes in need. The QIDP documents the review with date, findings and any changes made, and signs it.

When the strategy is changed, the QIDP updates the strategy with the individual and guardian, obtains signatures again, gives them the update, and replaces the copy at the residence within [2] business days.

All staff entries in the case record are dated, timed and signed under REC-02, with no blank entries, and corrections are made by single-line strike-through and initials. Electronic records follow the e-signature standards in REC-02.

Case records at the residence are kept in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system. Only staff with a need to know may use them, and guardian, individual and surveyor access follows REC-01 and REC-04.

The QIDP audits each record at least quarterly using a record checklist (current Personal Plan; Implementation Strategy signed and dated within 20 days; monthly reviews; consents; rights notice; health documents) and records deficiencies and the date corrected.

The Administrator reviews audit results quarterly and reports record deficiencies in the QA-01 review. When an individual leaves, the QIDP completes the discharge section, and records are retained and released as REC-04 requires.

responsibilities.duty: Opens and organizes the record, develops and updates the Implementation Strategy within timelines, performs the monthly review, and audits records quarterly.
Ensures records exist and are current for every individual and reviews audit results.
Follows the current Implementation Strategy at the residence and documents support delivered.
Keeps health information in the record current and reflects changes in health needs in the strategy.
Take part in developing the strategy, sign it, and receive copies.

documentation: Cumulative case record with table of contents
Written informed consent to participate
Prior service history
Personal Plan with provider's dated signature
Implementation Strategy on Form IL462-4470 signed and dated by individual and guardian
Record of delivery of strategy copies
Monthly QIDP review documentation
Quarterly record audits and corrective actions

policies.title: Human Rights Committee
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] Human Rights Committee members; the Administrator, QIDPs and staff who bring rights issues to the committee; all individuals served and their guardians
policies.purpose: To establish a Human Rights Committee that regularly reviews human rights issues and any rights restrictions affecting individuals, and to ensure each review is documented and followed up.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(2)(A) — Behavior management and human rights review; 115.320(c)(2)(B)(i)-(v) — Human Rights Committee duties; and 115.320(c)(2)(C)(i)-(iii) — Human Rights Committee membership.

115.320(c)(2)(A): [AGENCY NAME] has a Human Rights Committee that establishes or ensures a process for the periodic review of human rights issues involved in each individual's services and supports. Because the agency uses behavioral interventions, it also has a separate Behavior Management Committee (GPR-03). Each committee has at least five members. Members are not shared between the committees, except for a physician, APRN, registered professional nurse, or nurse practitioner/physician assistant.

115.320(c)(2)(B): The Committee (i) reviews at least annually the agency's policies, procedures and practices that could restrict individuals' rights; (ii) reviews at least every six months any practice that restricts a specific individual's rights; (iii) informs the agency of any complaints involving an individual's rights, any deficiencies, and any corrective actions; (iv) ensures individuals, guardians and natural supports, as desired, are included in meetings about their services and supports; and (v) maintains minutes that include attendance and a record of the decision made for each individual, with justification and intended outcome. When a restrictive intervention is approved, the minutes record the next review date.

115.320(c)(2)(C): The Committee has (i) at least five members; (ii) at least one person receiving services from the agency and/or an individual's family member or guardian; and (iii) at least one-third of its members who are not former employees of the agency, individuals or guardians of individuals formerly served, vendors providing products or services to the agency, or employees of other CILA providers or developmental disability programs.

The Committee protects the rights in Chapter II of the Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities Code (405 ILCS 5), the Rights of Individuals form (IL 462-1201), and 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.250. Seclusion, time-out and aversive procedures are never approved. Prone, supine and mechanical restraint are prohibited. Any other restraint is considered only under the conditions in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.245 and GPR-04. A modification of an HCBS setting right must meet 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F) and RTS-02.

definitions.definition: The committee of at least five members that reviews human rights issues and rights restrictions affecting individuals.
Any practice, rule or plan that limits an individual's rights, such as limits on access to belongings, food, visitors, money or movement.
An intervention that restricts an individual's rights or freedom and that must be approved by the committee with a next-review date.
Family, friends and others in the individual's life who give unpaid support, included in meetings as the individual desires.
A member who is not a former employee, a former individual or guardian, a vendor, or an employee of another CILA provider or DD program.

procedures: The Governing Body appoints at least five HRC members in writing. The membership roster lists each member's name, role and independence status, and the date appointed.

The Administrator confirms the roster includes at least one person receiving services from the agency and/or an individual's family member or guardian. For a five-member committee, at least two members must meet the independent-member test, and the roster shows this for each member.

The Administrator confirms no HRC member also sits on the Behavior Management Committee, except a physician, APRN, registered professional nurse, or nurse practitioner/physician assistant. A comparison of the two rosters is made at each appointment and annually.

The HRC meets at least quarterly and sooner when a restriction or rights complaint needs review. The chairperson sets the agenda and gives members and invited individuals and guardians at least [7] days notice, in accessible formats (RTS-04).

The QIDP lists every practice that restricts a specific individual's rights, with the next review date, and gives the list to the chairperson each quarter. Each such practice is reviewed at least every six months.

At least annually, the HRC reviews the agency's policies, procedures and practices that could restrict rights, including house rules, visitor and curfew rules, access to food, money handling and use of any monitoring. It records recommended changes and the Administrator's response.

For each proposed or continuing restriction, the QIDP presents the assessed need, less restrictive measures tried, the justification, the intended outcome, the plan to reduce or end it, and the individual's and guardian's informed consent, consistent with RTS-02. The HRC decides to approve, modify or deny.

The HRC invites the individual, the guardian and natural supports, as the individual desires, to meetings about the individual's services and supports, and helps with transportation, accessible materials and support to speak. Their input is recorded.
Members who have a conflict of interest, such as a member who is the guardian or supervisor of the individual under review, do not vote on that individual's matter. The minutes record the recusal.

The recording secretary writes minutes of each meeting that include attendance, and a record of the decision for each individual with the justification and intended outcome. When a restrictive intervention is approved, the minutes state the next review date.

The HRC informs the Administrator in writing, within [5] business days after each meeting, of any complaints involving an individual's rights, any deficiencies found, and the corrective actions recommended. Section GPR-06 applies to complaints and grievances.
The Administrator responds in writing within [10] business days with corrective actions and target dates, and the HRC tracks them to closure at its next meeting.

The HRC does not approve seclusion, time-out or aversive procedures. A request involving restraint other than prone, supine or mechanical restraint is referred to GPR-04 and is considered only when every condition in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.245 is met, including approval by the Behavior Management or Human Rights Committee and a plan to reduce and eliminate it.
Minutes and rosters are kept confidentially (REC-01) and are available for review by BALC and DDD. The Administrator reports HRC activity to the Governing Body and in the QA-01 review.

responsibilities.duty: Appoints the HRC, ensures membership requirements are met, and receives HRC reports.
Schedules and leads meetings, ensures minutes are kept and reviews of restrictions occur on time, and reports to the Administrator.
Supports the HRC, responds to its findings with corrective action, and checks that membership rules are met.
Presents restrictions and plans, keeps the restriction list with next-review dates, and includes individuals and guardians.
Review human rights issues objectively, decline to vote on conflicts, and keep information confidential.

documentation: HRC roster showing role and independence status of each member
Written appointment of members
HRC meeting notices and agendas
Minutes with attendance, individual decisions, justification, intended outcomes and next review dates
List of individual rights restrictions with review dates
Annual policy review record
Written reports to the Administrator and responses
Corrective action tracking log
Conflict-of-interest recusal records

policies.title: Behavior Management Committee and Positive Behavior Support
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] Behavior Management Committee members, QIDPs, nurses, clinicians and DSPs who develop, approve or carry out behavior strategies
policies.purpose: To make sure every behavior intervention is reviewed and approved by a qualified Behavior Management Committee before use, that positive supports are emphasized, and that any rights restriction also receives Human Rights Committee review.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(2)(D)(i)-(iv) — Behavior Management Committee duties and 115.320(c)(2)(E)(i)-(iii) — Behavior Management Committee composition.

Because [AGENCY NAME] uses behavioral interventions as specified in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.214, it maintains a Behavior Management Committee (BMC) of at least five members, separate from the Human Rights Committee (GPR-02).

115.320(c)(2)(D): The BMC (i) approves behavior interventions before they are put into use and reviews them at least every six months; (ii) reviews all behavior strategies at least annually and determines whether a rights restriction exists, and a plan with a rights restriction is also reviewed by the Human Rights Committee; (iii) maintains minutes that include attendance and a record of decisions made; and (iv) seeks input from individuals, guardians and natural supports as desired.

115.320(c)(2)(E): BMC members (i) include persons qualified to evaluate the appropriateness of proposed behavior management interventions; (ii) include a licensed professional qualified to evaluate the use of drugs when drugs are used to manage behavior; and (iii) include at least one member from outside the agency.

Behavior strategies emphasize positive supports and never use seclusion, time-out or aversive procedures (59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.250). Prone, supine and mechanical restraint are prohibited. Any other restraint is allowed only if all conditions of 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.245 are met, as set out in GPR-04. No intervention is used before BMC approval.

definitions.definition: The committee of at least five members that approves and reviews behavior interventions and strategies.
A written plan of positive supports and, where approved, other interventions to address behavior that affects an individual's safety or community life.
Supports that teach new skills, change the environment and reinforce desired behavior, based on understanding the purpose of the behavior.
A limit on an individual's rights that must be justified, consented to and reviewed under RTS-02.
A procedure meant to cause pain, discomfort or humiliation to change behavior, which is prohibited.

procedures: The Governing Body appoints at least five BMC members in writing. The roster lists each member's name, qualifications and role.

The Administrator ensures the roster includes persons qualified to evaluate whether proposed behavior management interventions are appropriate, for example a behavior analyst, psychologist, QIDP with behavior training, or other qualified clinician. Qualifications are on file for each member.
The Administrator ensures that at least one member is from outside the agency. The outside member's name and affiliation are recorded on the roster.

When any individual's plan includes a drug used to manage behavior, the Administrator ensures a licensed professional qualified to evaluate its use (for example a physician, psychiatrist or pharmacist) is a BMC member for that review. The name and license are recorded.

The Administrator confirms that no BMC member also serves on the Human Rights Committee, except a physician, APRN, registered professional nurse, or nurse practitioner/physician assistant. Rosters are compared at each appointment and annually.

The BMC meets at least quarterly and whenever a new intervention needs approval. Notice and agenda are given to members at least [7] days ahead. Individuals, guardians and natural supports are invited as the individual desires.

Before an intervention is used, the QIDP submits a written behavior strategy that includes the target behavior, assessment of its purpose and any medical cause, positive supports and skill teaching, the intervention, data collection method, and criteria for reducing or ending it.

The BMC reviews the strategy to decide whether it is appropriate and whether it emphasizes positive supports. It rejects any strategy that uses seclusion, time-out, aversive procedures, or prone, supine or mechanical restraint.
The BMC records approval, modification or denial of each intervention. No intervention is carried out before approval and staff are trained on it first (TRN-03).

For each strategy, the BMC determines whether a rights restriction exists and records the finding. A plan with a restriction is sent to the Human Rights Committee for review under GPR-02 and RTS-02, and is not carried out until both approvals and consents are on file.

If restraint other than prone, supine or mechanical restraint is proposed, the BMC applies the conditions in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.245. These include an immediate threat of serious physical harm, less restrictive measures shown to be ineffective, a Personal Plan modification approved by the individual or guardian and the Provider Support Team, specific staff training, no medical or psychological contraindication, and a plan to reduce and eliminate it. The BMC refers the matter to GPR-04 procedures.
The BMC seeks input from the individual, guardian and natural supports as desired before and during each review, and records their views and how the committee responded.

The BMC reviews every approved intervention at least every six months and reviews all behavior strategies at least annually. The QIDP brings data on frequency, severity, side effects and progress toward reduction, and the minutes record the next review date.
The recording secretary keeps minutes that include attendance and a record of each decision. Minutes are confidential (REC-01), and they are available to BALC and DDD.

The BMC reports to the Administrator within [5] business days of each meeting on approvals, denials and concerns. The Administrator reports summary data on behavior support and restraint to the Governing Body and in the QA-01 review.

responsibilities.duty: Appoints the BMC and ensures its membership requirements are met.
Schedules and leads meetings, ensures review timelines are met, and makes sure minutes are complete.
Prepares and presents behavior strategies and data, makes sure interventions are not used before approval, and arranges Human Rights Committee referral.
Confirms committee composition, supports committee work and acts on its findings.
Evaluates whether drugs used to manage behavior are appropriate and advises the BMC.
Uses only approved strategies as trained, collects behavior data and reports concerns.

Written appointment of members
Meeting notices and agendas
Minutes with attendance, decisions, justification, input from individuals and guardians, and next review dates
Written behavior strategies with approval dates
Six-month and annual review records
Rights-restriction determinations and Human Rights Committee referrals
Behavior and intervention data summaries
Reports to the Administrator and Governing Body

policies.title: Restraint, Seclusion, Time-Out and Aversive Procedures
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractual workers, volunteers, the Behavior Management Committee, the Human Rights Committee and every individual served by [AGENCY NAME] in any CILA site
policies.purpose: To protect each individual's right to be free from restraint, seclusion, time-out and aversive procedures. To set out the narrow, tightly controlled conditions under which any restraint other than prone, supine or mechanical restraint may ever be used. To make sure every use is approved, planned, reported, reviewed and reduced.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports individuals through positive, person-centered approaches and does not use restraint as a routine, convenience or disciplinary measure. In line with 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.245 and 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.250: (1) Prone restraint, supine restraint and mechanical restraint are prohibited. (2) Seclusion, time-out and aversive procedures are prohibited. (3) Any other restraint is permitted only if EVERY condition in Procedure 6 is met. (4) Individual rights are protected under Chapter II of the Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities Code (405 ILCS 5), except that seclusion is not permitted. (5) Individuals have the right to be free from abuse, neglect, exploitation, coercion and restraint. Any use of prone, supine or mechanical restraint is reported in CIRAS and to the DHS Office of the Inspector General (OIG). Any restraint of an individual that is not an approved modification in the Personal Plan is a critical incident and is handled under CI-01 and CI-02. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a copy of this restraint policy on file and available to the Department. This policy also supports the HCBS settings requirement that any modification of an individual's rights be supported by a specific assessed need, documented in the person-centered plan, and informed by consent (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F)). No official checklist items are assigned to this policy.

definitions.definition: As defined in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120. For this manual, any manual, physical or mechanical method that restricts an individual's freedom of movement. A physical escort or prompt that the individual can easily resist is not restraint.
Holding an individual face-down. Prohibited.
Holding an individual face-up on the back. Prohibited.
Use of a device, material or equipment to restrict movement. Prohibited.
Involuntary confinement of an individual alone in a room or area from which the individual is physically prevented from leaving. Prohibited.
Removing an individual from an activity or from positive reinforcement and placing them in a separate area as a consequence for behavior. Prohibited.

As defined in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120. For this manual, any procedure meant to cause pain, discomfort or humiliation, or to deprive the individual of food, sleep, personal items or other needs or rights, to change behavior. Prohibited.
As defined in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120. Using threats, pressure or loss of a right or service to force an individual's compliance.

The individual, the guardian (if any), the Independent Service Coordination (ISC) representative, agency staff and others the individual chooses, who develop and approve the Personal Plan and its modifications.

definitions.term: Behavior Management Committee (BMC) / Human Rights Committee (HRC)
definitions.definition: The agency committees described in GPR-03 and GPR-02 that review and approve behavior strategies and any rights modification.

procedures: The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] gives every employee, contractual worker and volunteer a copy of this policy at orientation (TRN-01 and TRN-04). Each signs an acknowledgment before working alone with individuals.

Staff must never use prone, supine or mechanical restraint, seclusion, time-out or any aversive procedure. This applies in every circumstance, including emergencies, and no one, including a guardian or family member, may authorize them.
Staff must also never use restraint, threats, loss of rights, withholding of food, belongings, visitors or activities, or other coercion as punishment or for staff convenience.

Staff prevent crises through the individual's Implementation Strategy and positive behavior supports (GPR-03, PCS-01 and PCS-03). They watch for triggers, offer choices and apply de-escalation steps written in the plan.

In a developing crisis, staff use verbal de-escalation, offer space, remove hazards and other people from the area, and call 911 when there is immediate danger. They call the on-call supervisor at [PHONE]. Staff do not physically hold or restrain an individual unless an approved plan allows it (see Procedure 6).

Restraint other than prone, supine or mechanical restraint may be written into an individual's plan only if ALL of the following are met and documented: (a) there is an immediate threat of serious physical harm to the individual or others; (b) less restrictive measures have been tried and proven ineffective; (c) the restraint is written as a modification in the Personal Plan and in the behavior strategy; (d) the individual or guardian and the Provider Support Team have approved the modification; (e) the BMC and HRC have reviewed and approved it; (f) the plan includes a written plan to reduce and eliminate the restraint; (g) staff who may use it have been trained in the specific restraint technique; and (h) the agency has documented that there is no medical or psychological contraindication, with input from the individual's physician and a qualified clinician.

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] checks the file for all eight conditions in Procedure 6 before any approved restraint is added to a plan. If any is missing, the restraint is not authorized and may not be used.

Only staff with documented, current training in the specific approved restraint may use it, and only as the plan describes. The agency records the trainer, date, technique and competency check in the personnel record (STF-05).

After every use of an approved restraint, the staff member who used it notifies the on-call supervisor immediately, makes sure the individual is safe and checks for injury. If there is injury or doubt, staff call 911 or arrange medical care (HLT-03). Staff complete an incident report before the end of the shift.

The Program Supervisor reviews the incident within one business day. The review looks at what led to it, how long it lasted, whether the individual was safe, and whether the plan was followed. The review is sent to the BMC, HRC and Provider Support Team.

For any use of prone, supine or mechanical restraint, and for any restraint outside an approved Personal Plan, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee reports it to the DHS OIG and enters it in CIRAS within the time frames in CI-02. The individual's guardian is notified, and law enforcement is notified when required (CI-02).

Staff involved in a restraint that was not in the Personal Plan are removed from direct work with that individual until the incident is reviewed. They complete remediation training when the Department or the agency requires it, and completion is documented in the personnel file. Findings of abuse are handled under GPR-05 and STF-06.

The BMC reviews every approved restraint plan at least quarterly. It looks at frequency and trends and records progress toward reducing and eliminating the restraint. The BMC reports concerns to the HRC.

Each month, the Quality Assurance coordinator compiles data on all restraint-related incidents and on any use of prohibited practices. It is reported to the governing body and used in the QA review (QA-01 and CI-01).
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews this policy at least annually and keeps the current copy on file at the main office and at each site, available to the Department and BALC.

Individuals, guardians and staff may report any suspected improper restraint or use of a prohibited practice to the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], the HRC, the Guardianship and Advocacy Commission, Equip for Equality, the DHS OIG or the Department. Retaliation is prohibited (GPR-06).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, receives restraint and prohibited-practice data, and makes sure the agency does not permit prohibited practices.
Ensures that all conditions are met before any restraint is authorized, files OIG and CIRAS reports, and arranges remediation.

responsibilities.role: Behavior Management Committee and Human Rights Committee
responsibilities.duty: Review and approve behavior strategies and any restraint modification, and review use at least quarterly.
Reviews each incident within one business day, supervises staff, and confirms staff training.
Use positive supports and de-escalation, never use prohibited practices, and report and document any incident.
Provides health input on medical contraindications and checks the individual after any restraint.

documentation: Signed staff acknowledgment of this policy
Personal Plan modification and behavior strategy with signed approval of the individual or guardian and Provider Support Team
BMC and HRC approval records and the written plan to reduce and eliminate restraint
Documentation of no medical or psychological contraindication
Staff training and competency records for the specific restraint
Incident reports, supervisor reviews, and OIG and CIRAS confirmations
Remediation training records
Quarterly BMC review minutes
Current copy of this restraint policy on file

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention, Reporting and Handling Process
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractual workers, volunteers, board members and others who have contact with individuals served by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect individuals from abuse, neglect and exploitation, and to make sure every allegation is reported, acted on, investigated and tracked. This includes notice to the individual and their guardian or parent within 24 hours.
policies.policy: This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(3)(A) (Abuse, neglect, and exploitation). [AGENCY NAME] has and uses a process for reporting and handling instances of abuse, neglect and exploitation in accordance with applicable standards, regulations and laws. Abuse, neglect and exploitation have the meanings in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 50.10 (adopted by 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120). The agency notifies the individual allegedly abused, neglected or exploited, and their guardian or parent, of the allegation within 24 hours after receiving the allegation. The agency reports to the DHS Office of the Inspector General (OIG) within 4 hours of discovery (see CI-02). Staff complete OIG Rule 50 abuse and neglect training at orientation and every two years. Every employee, contractual worker and volunteer must report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately. The agency never retaliates against a person who reports. The agency does not accept, ignore or privately resolve an allegation.

definitions.definition: As defined in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 50.10 (adopted by reference in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120). The Part 50 definitions control, and staff training uses the current text.
Any report, suspicion, observation or disclosure that abuse, neglect or exploitation may have occurred, whether from the individual, a staff member, a family member, a visitor or anyone else.
As defined in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120. Critical incidents include abuse, neglect and exploitation as defined in Part 50.
The moment any agency staff member or volunteer first sees, hears of or suspects the incident.
The DHS Office of the Inspector General.
The Department's critical incident reporting and analysis system.

procedures: At orientation and every two years, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] makes sure each employee, contractual worker and volunteer completes OIG Rule 50 abuse and neglect training and signs a statement that they understand the duty to report (TRN-04, VOL-01). Completion dates are kept in the personnel record.

Any person who sees or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately protects the individual and any others at risk. Staff separate the individual from the alleged source of harm. If the alleged source is a staff member, that person is removed from contact with individuals at once.

Staff get medical care at once for any injury or health need and call 911 when there is immediate danger or serious injury (HLT-03). Staff preserve evidence, including clothing, the scene and equipment. They do not clean, alter or discard anything related to the allegation.
The person who discovers the allegation notifies the on-call supervisor and the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] at [PHONE] without delay, and in any event before the end of the shift.

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee reports the allegation to the OIG within 4 hours of discovery, using the OIG reporting line [DHS OIG HOTLINE NUMBER]. The agency enters the required report in CIRAS and notifies law enforcement where required (CI-02).
The person making the report records the date and time of discovery, the date and time of the OIG report, the report number, and the name of the person who received the report.

Within 24 hours after receiving the allegation, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee notifies the individual allegedly abused, neglected or exploited, and their guardian or parent, of the allegation. If the first attempt does not reach them, staff keep trying and record every attempt. Notice is given in the individual's preferred communication method (RTS-04) and recorded in the chronological record.

The agency does not ask the alleged victim or witnesses to write statements or repeat their account unless OIG or law enforcement instructs it. Staff offer emotional support and access to advocacy, including the Guardianship and Advocacy Commission and Equip for Equality (GPR-06).

The agency follows all OIG instructions and cooperates fully with OIG, law enforcement and the Department. Agency staff do not interview the individual or accused in a way that interferes with an OIG or police investigation. When OIG directs the agency to investigate, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] assigns a trained investigator who is not involved in the incident and follows the direction in CI-01.

Staff accused of abuse, neglect or exploitation are removed from direct contact with individuals pending the outcome as the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] directs. Any prohibited practice under GPR-04 is treated as an allegation under this policy.

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews the individual's safety plan within one business day. The review looks at supervision, health and the living arrangement, and may recommend a Provider Support Team meeting (PCS-02).

When OIG or the agency substantiates a finding, the agency takes corrective and disciplinary action as the law and the finding require, including termination. It reports to the Health Care Worker Registry when required (STF-02 and STF-03) and updates the individual's plan as needed.

The agency never retaliates against any individual, employee or volunteer who reports or cooperates in an investigation. Retaliation is grounds for discipline, up to and including termination (STF-06).

The Quality Assurance coordinator logs every allegation, report date, notification time, outcome and corrective action in the incident tracking system. The coordinator reviews trends at least quarterly and reports them to the governing body (CI-01, QA-01).

Individuals and guardians receive information about how to report concerns at entry and annually. This includes the Rights of Individuals form (GPR-06) and the OIG hotline and other contacts posted in a place accessible to individuals at each site.
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews this policy at least annually.

responsibilities.role: Every employee, contractual worker and volunteer
responsibilities.duty: Protects the individual, reports suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately, and preserves evidence.
Receives the report, makes sure the individual is safe and removes any accused staff member from contact.
Reports to OIG within 4 hours, ensures notice to the individual and guardian within 24 hours, directs any agency investigation and follows up on corrective action.
Tracks and analyzes allegations and outcomes and reports to the governing body.
Reviews trend data and makes sure the agency uses this process.

documentation: OIG Rule 50 training records at orientation and every two years
Signed staff statement on duty to report
Incident report with date and time of discovery
OIG report number, time of report and CIRAS entry
Record of notification of the individual and guardian or parent within 24 hours, including attempts
Investigation file and findings
Corrective action and disciplinary records
Allegation tracking log and quarterly trend reports

policies.title: Rights Complaints and Grievances
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractual workers, volunteers, the Human Rights Committee, and every individual and guardian served by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give every individual and guardian a clear, accessible, retaliation-free way to raise complaints about rights. To make sure each person receives and understands the Rights of Individuals form and knows how to reach outside advocates.
policies.policy: This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(3)(B) (rights complaints and the Rights of Individuals form [IL 462-1201]). In addition to abuse, neglect and exploitation (GPR-05), [AGENCY NAME] has and uses a process for reporting and handling complaints regarding individual rights. The agency shares and explains the current Rights of Individuals form [IL 462-1201] with the individual and/or guardian when the individual enters the CILA program and annually thereafter, as required by 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.250. Rights are protected under Chapter II of the Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities Code (405 ILCS 5), except that seclusion is not permitted. Each individual may contact the Guardianship and Advocacy Commission (GAC), Equip for Equality, the DHS Office of the Inspector General (OIG), the Department and the agency's Human Rights Committee. Staff offer help in making those contacts and give each individual the address and telephone number of GAC, OIG, the Department and Equip for Equality. Rights complaints are reviewed by the Human Rights Committee (GPR-02). No individual, guardian, employee or volunteer will face retaliation for making a complaint. This is consistent with the person's rights under 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4).

definitions.definition: Any oral or written statement by an individual, guardian, family member, advocate or staff member that an individual's rights were denied, restricted or not respected.
A rights complaint that the complainant is not satisfied has been resolved, or a request for formal review.
The Department's current form describing individual rights, shared and explained at entry and annually.
The agency committee that reviews rights complaints, rights restrictions and related concerns (GPR-02).
Any adverse action, threat, loss of service or privilege, or change in treatment because someone made a complaint or helped with one.

procedures: At entry, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee gives the individual and guardian a copy of the current Rights of Individuals form [IL 462-1201], explains it in plain language and in the individual's preferred communication method (RTS-04), and answers questions. The individual and/or guardian signs to show it was shared and explained.

At the same time, staff give each individual the address and telephone number of GAC, OIG, the Department and Equip for Equality, and tell the person they may also contact the agency's HRC. Staff offer to help the individual place calls, write letters or arrange visits. The contact list is [GAC ADDRESS AND PHONE], [OIG ADDRESS AND PHONE], [DEPARTMENT ADDRESS AND PHONE] and [EQUIP FOR EQUALITY ADDRESS AND PHONE].

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] repeats the sharing and explanation of the form and contact information at least annually, at or before the annual Personal Plan meeting, and records it in the record (REC-03).

The agency posts the rights summary and complaint contacts in a place at each site where individuals can see them without staff help. Staff re-explain whenever an individual asks or a rights concern arises.

Any individual, guardian or other person may make a rights complaint orally or in writing to any staff member, the Program Supervisor, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the HRC. A person may also use a grievance box, email to [EMAIL ADDRESS] or phone [PHONE]. Staff help the individual put the complaint in writing if the individual wants.

Any staff member who receives a rights complaint records it the same day on the complaint form, without changing the meaning, and gives it to the Program Supervisor by the next business day. Staff must not try to talk the individual out of making a complaint.

The Program Supervisor acknowledges the complaint to the complainant within 2 business days. The complainant is told how the process works and that they may get help from any advocate of their choice.
If the complaint alleges abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Program Supervisor follows GPR-05 at once. If it involves a restraint or prohibited practice, GPR-04 also applies.

Within 10 business days, the Program Supervisor or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] looks into the complaint, works to resolve it and gives the complainant a written response. The response states what was found and what will be done. Immediate corrections are made when a right is being denied without proper due process (RTS-02).

A complaint about a rights restriction, or one that remains unresolved, goes to the HRC for review at its next meeting or sooner if the issue is urgent. The complainant may attend or have a representative attend. The HRC decision is given to the complainant in writing.
If the complainant is still not satisfied, the agency informs the person of the right to contact GAC, Equip for Equality, OIG or the Department, and helps with the contact when asked.
No staff member may retaliate against anyone who raises a complaint. Suspected retaliation is reported to the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and treated as a rights violation and possible abuse under GPR-05.
The Program Supervisor updates the individual's Personal Plan or Implementation Strategy when a complaint shows the plan needs to change, and informs the Provider Support Team (PCS-02).

The Quality Assurance coordinator logs every complaint, date, response, outcome and corrective action, reviews trends at least quarterly and reports them to the HRC and governing body (QA-01, GOV-02).
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews this policy at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the Rights of Individuals form and contact information are shared at entry and annually, and that complaints are resolved without retaliation.
Acknowledges and investigates complaints, gives written responses and refers to the HRC.
Accept complaints, offer help to contact advocates, and report all complaints promptly.
Reviews rights complaints and restrictions and recommends corrective action.
Tracks complaints and reports trends.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment that the Rights of Individuals form [IL 462-1201] was shared and explained at entry and annually
Record that GAC, OIG, Department and Equip for Equality contact information was provided
Rights complaint forms and acknowledgments
Written responses and HRC decisions
Complaint log and quarterly trend reports
Record of help provided to contact outside advocates

policies.title: Nondiscrimination, Admission Policies and Procedures, Referral and Respite
policies.applies_to: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], admission and program staff, and all employees involved in referral, intake, admission or respite
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits and serves individuals without discrimination, uses written admission policies that are available for review, and handles referral and respite in line with Illinois CILA rules.
policies.policy: This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(4)(A) (Admission requirements: nondiscrimination) and 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(4)(B) (Admission policies and procedures set forth in writing and available for review). (A) [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission to or the provision of needed services on the basis of race, color, sex, religion (creed), gender identity, gender expression, age, national origin (ancestry), ethnicity, disability, marital status, sexual orientation or military status in any of its activities or operations. This is consistent with Title VI (42 USC 2000d) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101 et seq.). (B) These admission policies and procedures are in writing and are available for review by individuals, guardians, referral sources, the Department and BALC at [ADDRESS]. Under 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.210, an individual must be at least 18 with a developmental disability and need CILA services and a supervised living arrangement. The agency may request an age waiver for an individual who is at least 17.5. No otherwise qualified individual is denied placement solely on the basis of diagnosis, and the agency's lack of capacity for a particular disability does not make an individual ineligible. Respite follows 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.205.

definitions.definition: The point at which an eligible individual moves into a CILA site operated by [AGENCY NAME] and begins receiving services.
The Independent Service Coordination agency that enrolls individuals in PUNS and is the intake and referral channel for waiver services.
Short-term residential support provided to an eligible individual who is not a resident of the home, under 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.205.
The individual, guardian, ISC representative, agency staff and others the individual chooses, who plan and approve services.
The Department's approval for an individual who is at least 17.5 but under 18 to participate.

procedures: The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] provides a copy of this policy to the governing body, staff involved in admission, ISC agencies on request, and anyone who asks. The policy is available for review at [ADDRESS] and at each site (115.320(c)(4)(B)).

Referrals come through ISC agencies. The agency also accepts a request directly from an individual or guardian and directs them to their ISC agency to coordinate funding and services. Referral sources receive the same written information.

On receiving a referral, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee records the date, source and individual's name, and responds to the ISC or referral source within [NUMBER] business days. Referrals for people in crisis (homelessness, abuse or neglect) are acted on promptly, with the ISC's Crisis Transition Plan and Funding Request used as the starting point.

Staff check eligibility: the individual must be at least 18 (or at least 17.5 with an age waiver request), have a developmental disability, and need CILA services and a supervised living arrangement. Documents such as the ISC eligibility determination are placed in the record.

No referral is declined or ranked based on race, color, sex, religion (creed), gender identity, gender expression, age, national origin (ancestry), ethnicity, disability, marital status, sexual orientation or military status. Staff do not ask questions or apply criteria on these characteristics.

The agency does not deny placement to an otherwise qualified individual solely based on diagnosis. If the agency lacks capacity or experience with a disability, that does not make the individual ineligible. The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] documents the specific supports needed and requests additional supports through the Provider Support Team (PCS-02), and consults the ISC agency and the Department.

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and Program Supervisor arrange a visit to the home so the individual and guardian can see the home, meet housemates and staff, and ask questions. The individual's preferences and compatibility with the home are considered while respecting nondiscrimination.

If the agency is not able to admit an individual, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] records the reason in writing and gives it to the referral source and the individual or guardian. The reason must not be based on a characteristic listed in Procedure 5 or solely on diagnosis. The agency offers help in finding other options.

Before admission, the individual or guardian gives informed consent to participate in the CILA, which is documented (RTS-03, REC-03). The agency explains the Rights of Individuals form (GPR-06), the house rules, the residency agreement and the complaint process.

Following admission, the individual's ISC completes Discovery and develops the Personal Plan within 30 calendar days after the person begins DDD Waiver services. The Program Supervisor works with the ISC and Provider Support Team to create the Implementation Strategy (PCS-01, GPR-01).
For respite, before the stay begins, the agency obtains a physician's statement that the individual has no contagious disease.

Also before respite, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or Program Supervisor documents that the individual will not jeopardize the health or safety of others in the home, taking account of the current residents' needs.

Respite may last up to two weeks. Respite longer than two weeks needs Department approval before the initial two weeks end, and is allowed only in emergencies. The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] requests approval in writing and keeps the Department's response.

During respite, staff follow the individual's current Personal Plan or support information, medication orders and rights, and complete the same documentation as for residents. A respite record is kept for each stay.
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews referral and admission data annually for patterns of unfair treatment and reports to the governing body (GOV-01, QA-01). The policy is reviewed at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the written admission policy and reviews referral and admission data.
Makes admission decisions in line with this policy, documents any reason an individual cannot be admitted, and requests respite approvals and age waivers.
Arranges visits, assesses compatibility and documents respite safety determinations.
Obtains and reviews the physician statement for respite.
Enrolls individuals, makes referrals, and completes Discovery and the Personal Plan within 30 days of the start of services.

documentation: Written admission policy available for review
Referral log with dates and outcomes
Eligibility documents and any age waiver request
Written reason for any non-admission
Informed consent to participate
Signed acknowledgment of the Rights of Individuals form
Physician statement of no contagious disease for respite
Documentation that respite will not jeopardize others' health or safety
Department approval for respite over two weeks
Respite stay records

policies.title: Life Safety, Code Compliance, Residential Environment and Siting
policies.applies_to: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], program and maintenance staff, and all employees at every CILA site owned, leased or controlled by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every CILA site is safe, code-compliant, accessible and sited as the rules require. Each site must also be a home-like community setting that supports individuals' integration, privacy and control.
policies.policy: This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(5) (Compliance with life safety standards and requirements). All program facilities of [AGENCY NAME] are in compliance with applicable State licensure requirements and local ordinances with regard to fire, building, zoning, sanitation, health and safety requirements. This policy also applies 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.300 (environmental management), 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.310 (geographic location), 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.200 (description of settings and services) and 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.410 (license application). Each CILA serves eight or fewer individuals. The agency will not occupy or admit individuals to a site until it has been inspected by BALC as required and the fire clearance and other required documents are in place. Settings are physically accessible, and communal areas meet ADA standards (42 USC 12101 et seq.). Provider-owned or controlled sites meet the HCBS settings requirements in 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(A)-(E).

definitions.definition: A community integrated living arrangement serving eight or fewer individuals with a developmental disability, as defined in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120.
A residence that the agency owns, leases or otherwise controls.
The Office of the State Fire Marshal, which provides fire inspection and clearance.
The Department's approval to locate a new site in a position otherwise restricted by 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.310.
The plan covering disasters and public health crises, reviewed annually (ENV-01).

procedures: Before leasing, buying or taking possession of any site, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] checks the address against the siting rules and records the result. A new provider-owned or controlled site may not be adjacent to, across from, diagonal to or behind another waiver-funded residential or day site of the same provider unless a waiver is granted.

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms that the site is not in a building that provides inpatient institutional treatment and that Department-funded CILAs owned or controlled by CILA providers make up no more than 25% of the units in the building.

If a siting waiver is needed, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] files the waiver request before leasing, buying or taking possession of the site and keeps the Department's written decision. The agency does not take possession of a restricted site without a waiver.

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms zoning, local building, fire, sanitation and health requirements with the local authorities and keeps written confirmation and any permits or occupancy documents on file.

Before an individual moves in, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] provides the documents BALC needs for the site inspection and asks BALC to submit the request to OSFM for fire clearance. BALC's site inspection takes place after fire clearances and other required documents are received. The agency allows no occupancy until BALC's inspection and OSFM clearance are complete.
The agency notifies BALC and the Department of any change in ownership within 60 business days (59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.410) and notifies BALC before any change of site address.

The site is made physically accessible for each individual living there, and communal areas meet ADA standards. The Program Supervisor reviews accessibility needs at admission and when an individual's mobility changes, and arranges modifications (PCS-02).

Each site is set up as a home. Individuals have a lockable bedroom door, with only the appropriate staff holding keys, and choice of roommates where shared bedrooms exist. They may decorate their own rooms, have visitors at any time as their plans allow, and control their daily schedules, consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(A)-(E) and RTS-01. Any modification is handled under RTS-02.
The Program Supervisor keeps copies of local and State health, sanitation and environment inspections at the site and makes them available to BALC and the Department.

At each site, staff keep an operational telephone accessible. They post the site phone number and the nearest poison control center number next to it. At least one approved fire extinguisher with a current annual inspection tag is kept at each site.
A Red Cross-standard first aid kit is kept at each site. The Program Supervisor checks and restocks it quarterly and records the date.

The agency maintains a disaster preparedness plan covering disasters and public health crises and reviews it annually (ENV-01). Fire drills include actual evacuation to safe areas. Staff are trained in the location of extinguishers, first aid kits and evacuation routes, and each new individual is trained within 30 days of moving in (TRN-02). Records are available at the site to the Department's Division of Developmental Disabilities and BALC.
The Program Supervisor records any deficiency found in a drill, inspection or walk-through, assigns a corrective action with a due date and records completion (QA-02).

The Program Supervisor inspects each site monthly for hazards, repairs, cleanliness, hot water temperature and accessibility (TRN-02, ENV-02), and records the result. Urgent hazards are corrected immediately, and individuals are moved if the site is unsafe.
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews this policy and site compliance at least annually and reports to the governing body (GOV-01).

responsibilities.duty: Approves site acquisition and receives compliance reports.
Checks siting rules, files waivers, coordinates BALC and OSFM inspections, and ensures code compliance.
Performs monthly site checks, keeps inspection records and safety equipment, and records corrective actions.
Know safety equipment and evacuation routes and report hazards immediately.
Makes repairs and modifications and provides inspection certificates.

documentation: Siting review and any waiver request and decision
Zoning, building, fire, sanitation and health approvals and permits
BALC inspection results and OSFM clearance
Copies of local and State health, sanitation and environment inspections kept at the site
Fire extinguisher annual inspection tag
Quarterly first aid kit checks
Disaster preparedness plan and annual review
Drill and training records
Monthly site inspection logs
Corrective action records
Accessibility assessments

policies.title: Visits by Protection and Advocacy Groups
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractual workers and volunteers, and every individual and guardian served by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure Department-authorized protection and advocacy groups can visit provider-owned or controlled living arrangements, with the consent of the individual or guardian, and that visits are respected and documented.
policies.policy: This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(6) (Visits to programs). [AGENCY NAME] ensures that Department-authorized individual protection and advocacy interest groups are permitted, with the consent of the individual or guardian, to visit provider-owned or controlled living arrangements. Staff never refuse, delay, obstruct or discourage a visit that the individual or guardian has agreed to. The agency respects each person's privacy during the visit. Individuals may also contact the Guardianship and Advocacy Commission, Equip for Equality, the DHS Office of the Inspector General, the Department and the agency's Human Rights Committee, and staff offer help in doing so (59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.250 and GPR-06).

definitions.definition: An organization authorized by the Department to advocate for and protect the interests of individuals with developmental disabilities, such as those named in the Rights of Individuals form. Examples are the Guardianship and Advocacy Commission and Equip for Equality.
A CILA residence that [AGENCY NAME] owns, leases or controls.
Agreement by the individual or the individual's guardian to meet with or be visited by the group, given freely and without pressure.

procedures: At orientation, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] trains all staff on this policy. Each staff member must understand that authorized advocacy groups may visit and that no one may block, discourage or retaliate over a visit.

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] posts this policy and the names and contact information of advocacy groups ([GAC ADDRESS AND PHONE] and [EQUIP FOR EQUALITY ADDRESS AND PHONE]) at each site where individuals can see them, and shares them with each individual and guardian at entry and annually (GPR-06).

When a representative of an advocacy group arrives or calls to request a visit, the staff member on duty greets the visitor courteously, asks for the visitor's name, organization and identification, and contacts the on-call supervisor at [PHONE] at once. This verification must not delay entry unreasonably.

The on-call supervisor or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms that the group is authorized by the Department, using the group's documentation or by contacting the Department or BALC at 312-814-5310 if there is doubt.

Staff ask each individual the visitor wishes to see whether they agree to the visit, in the individual's preferred communication method, and offer support to help the person decide. Where an individual has a guardian with authority, the agency contacts the guardian promptly for consent and does not delay or discourage the visit.

If the individual or guardian has consented, staff make the visit possible, offer a private space such as a bedroom, living room or other area the individual chooses, and do not listen in or stay unless asked.

If the individual or guardian declines, staff tell the visitor politely and accurately that consent was not given for that person. The decision is respected and recorded, and the visitor is offered the ability to make contact again.

Staff do not read, screen or restrict the advocacy group's access to an individual who has consented, and do not ask the group to leave early. Staff make sure the visit does not put any other individual's privacy at risk and show visitors only those areas they have consent to enter.

Staff record each visit in a visit log: the date, time, visitor name and organization, individuals seen, who gave consent and when the visitor left. The log records consent decisions but not the private content of the conversation.
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews the visit log monthly and any concern raised by a visit. The agency cooperates in good faith, makes corrections, and reports concerns to the HRC (GPR-02).

No staff member may retaliate against any individual, guardian or employee because of a visit or something said in a visit. Any suspected retaliation is reported to the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and handled under GPR-05 and GPR-06.
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews this policy at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures visits are allowed, verifies authorization when needed, trains staff and reviews the visit log.
Confirms authorization, supports consent discussions and ensures privacy during the visit.
Greet visitors, ask for consent, support the individual's decision, and record the visit.
Reviews concerns arising from visits.

documentation: Staff training record on this policy
Posted advocacy group contact information
Visit log showing date, visitor, consent and individuals seen
Record of guardian consent where needed
Record of verification of the group's authorization when needed
HRC review notes on any concerns

policies.title: Remote Monitoring and Supports; Authorized Electronic Monitoring
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] CILA sites, the Administrator, QIDP, Nurse, Provider Support Team members and direct support staff
policies.purpose: To state whether [AGENCY NAME] offers remote monitoring and supports, to set the conditions that must be met before any remote support is used, and to keep authorized electronic monitoring (a device in an individual's room) separate from remote supports and subject to its own law, 210 ILCS 165.
policies.policy: This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(c)(7) (Remote Monitoring and Supports). Remote monitoring and supports may be provided by CILA agencies under 305 ILCS 5/12-21.21, as determined by the Division of Developmental Disabilities (DDD). [AGENCY NAME] does not offer remote monitoring and supports at the time of licensure. The agency will not use or bill for remote monitoring or remote supports unless (1) DDD has determined that the agency may provide the service, (2) the Governing Body has approved the service in writing, and (3) each individual's use is based on a written assessment that identifies, at a minimum, the risks that bear on whether remote monitoring and supports are appropriate for that individual. If the agency later offers the service, all steps below apply before the first use. Remote monitoring and supports may never replace continuous supervision or support where the individual's Personal Plan and Implementation Strategy require staff to be physically on-site, and may never be used for staff convenience. Authorized electronic monitoring, meaning placement of a monitoring device in an individual's room, is governed by the Authorized Electronic Monitoring in Community-Integrated Living Arrangements and Developmental Disability Facilities Act (210 ILCS 165) and not by the remote-supports process in this policy. No camera, audio device or other monitoring device may be placed in any bedroom, bathroom or other private space except as that Act allows. Any monitoring that limits an individual's privacy is treated as a modification of the Personal Plan, with informed consent and review by the Human Rights Committee (GPR-02) before it starts.

definitions.definition: Services delivered through technology so that staff can monitor or support an individual from a different location, as permitted under 305 ILCS 5/12-21.21 and as determined by DDD. This is not the same as authorized electronic monitoring.
Placement of an electronic monitoring device in an individual's room under 210 ILCS 165, as defined in 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120.
Staff physically on-site at all hours the individuals are present unless the Personal Plan and Implementation Strategy say otherwise (59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120).
The individual, guardian, Independent Service Coordination (ISC) staff, QIDP and other persons who plan and review the individual's supports.
Agreement given voluntarily by the individual or guardian after the purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives have been explained in a way the person can understand (59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.120).

procedures: The Administrator confirms in writing with DDD whether [AGENCY NAME] may offer remote monitoring and supports under 305 ILCS 5/12-21.21 and keeps the DDD determination in the agency's administrative file. Until that determination is in the file and the Governing Body has approved the service, no remote support is used and this policy's "does not offer" statement stands.

If the service is approved, the Governing Body records its approval in the minutes and the Administrator updates the program description, staffing pattern (STF-04) and the Quality Assurance Plan (QA-01) to cover remote supports.

Remote supports are considered only when the individual, guardian or Provider Support Team raises them as an option or when an assessment suggests they may increase independence. Staff may not propose them to reduce staffing cost or for staff convenience.

The QIDP, with the Nurse where health risks are involved, completes a written assessment for the individual. At a minimum it identifies the risks important in deciding whether remote monitoring and supports are appropriate, including medical, behavioral, wandering and elopement, fire and emergency evacuation, abuse and neglect, and technology-failure risks.
The assessment also records the individual's preferences, ability to use or tolerate the technology, the less intrusive alternatives considered, and the effect on privacy and community integration.

The QIDP convenes the Provider Support Team to review the assessment. The team decides whether remote supports are appropriate, which supports will be used, and the times and locations they cover. The decision and each member's view are documented.

If the team decides to proceed, the QIDP writes the remote support into the Personal Plan and Implementation Strategy (Form IL462-4470), stating the outcome supported, the technology, the hours, any in-person backup and the response procedure when the technology fails or an alert occurs.

The QIDP explains the proposal to the individual and guardian in plain language, and in the individual's preferred communication method, covering what is seen or heard, who can see or hear it, how long information is kept and the right to decline or withdraw.

The individual and guardian give written informed consent before the first use. The QIDP files the signed consent in the record. A refusal or later withdrawal of consent is honored, and the agency continues or restores in-person supports at once.

Where the remote support restricts privacy, the QIDP documents it as a Personal Plan modification, using the assessed need, the less intrusive methods tried, the time limit, and the method for collecting and reviewing data. The QIDP then refers it to the Human Rights Committee (GPR-02) and to the restriction process (RTS-02). The support does not start until the review is complete.

The Administrator ensures that no device is placed in a bedroom or bathroom under the remote-supports process. Any request for a monitoring device in an individual's room is handled only as authorized electronic monitoring under 210 ILCS 165, with the consent and privacy protections that Act requires. The QIDP documents that consent in the record and the Administrator notifies the Human Rights Committee.

The Administrator restricts access to live feeds, recordings, alerts and data to named staff. Information is handled as confidential record information under REC-01 and RTS-05 and is not shared beyond persons authorized by the individual or guardian or by law.

The Administrator trains staff who operate or respond to the technology before they do so (TRN-03) and confirms that staff on duty can reach the individual quickly. Staff test the equipment and log the check [DAILY or as set by the Administrator].

The QIDP reviews each remote support at least monthly with the Implementation Strategy review, and the Provider Support Team reassesses it at least annually and whenever the individual's needs, health or behavior change. The reassessment is documented. Remote support stops if the assessment no longer supports it or consent is withdrawn.

Any technology failure, privacy breach, missed alert or harm linked to a remote support is reported as a critical incident under CI-01 and CI-02 and is reviewed in the quality assurance process (QA-01).
The Administrator reports the number of individuals using remote supports, incidents and consents to the Governing Body at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether the agency will offer remote supports once DDD has determined it may, and reviews annual use and incident data.
Obtains and files the DDD determination, ensures device and data controls, keeps electronic monitoring separate from remote supports, and ensures staff training.

Completes the risk assessment, leads the Provider Support Team review, writes the plan language, obtains written informed consent, refers privacy-limiting uses to the Human Rights Committee and reviews each use monthly.
Contributes health and medical risk information to the assessment and reviews health-related alerts.
Reviews any monitoring that restricts privacy before it starts and at each review period.
Operate and respond to approved technology as trained, preserve privacy, and report failures, misuse or concerns.

documentation: DDD determination that the agency may offer remote monitoring and supports, and Governing Body approval
Individual risk assessment and Provider Support Team decision
Personal Plan and Implementation Strategy language for the remote support
Written informed consent, or documented refusal or withdrawal
Human Rights Committee review and restriction or modification documentation
Consent and privacy documentation for any authorized electronic monitoring under 210 ILCS 165
Equipment check logs, access lists and staff training records
Monthly Implementation Strategy review notes and annual reassessment
Incident reports and annual Governing Body summary

policies.title: Direct Support Professional Orientation, Competency, Written Training Plan and Ongoing Development
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals and every paraprofessional, contractual worker and volunteer with responsibility for direct care; the Administrator, QIDP, Nurse and Training Coordinator
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who provides direct care at [AGENCY NAME] shows competence in the required training areas before working unsupervised, keeps developing skills after orientation, and that all training is documented and ready for review by BALC and DDD.
policies.policy: This policy meets 59 Ill. Adm. Code 115.320(d)(1) (orientation and demonstrated competence), 115.320(d)(2) (ongoing employee development), 115.320(d)(3) (training documented and available to BALC and DDD) and 115.320(d)(4) (written training plan). Direct service professionals and any other persons, including paraprofessional, contractual workers and volunteers, with responsibility for direct care must demonstrate competence in the training areas listed in 115.320(d)(1)(A) through (M) as part of an orientation program. Anyone without previous experience in direct service receives training and demonstrates competence before unsupervised responsibility for direct service, unless trained employees are on site and available for on-the-job training. Training and competence are documented in the employee record. Anyone who gives direct care more than 20% of the time is trained as a Direct Support Professional (DSP). First aid/CPR and OIG Rule 50 abuse and neglect training are renewed every two years. After orientation, each direct service employee takes part in ongoing development under the agency's employee development plan. All training records are kept so that they are readily available to BALC and DDD. [AGENCY NAME] has enough trained staff to cover expected and unexpected absences. The agency uses DSP and QIDP training programs approved by DDD after IMPACT enrollment.
